screens.title: Advanced Security Auditing and Formal Verification
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we’ll explore the advanced layers of smart contract assurance that go beyond normal unit testing. You already know how to write tests, but tests only show the presence of a bug under specific inputs. Here we will study professional audits, automated static analysis with tools like Slither, dynamic tools such as fuzzers, and the highest-assurance approach: formal verification. You will learn what each technique promises, where it fits in the development lifecycle, and the trade-offs — cost, time, required expertise, and types of bugs each method is best at finding. We’ll also follow a small hands-on workflow: run Slither on a deliberately vulnerable wallet contract, interpret the findings, apply fixes using secure patterns, and re-run tools to confirm remediation. By the end of this chapter you’ll be able to choose which measures are appropriate for different risk levels, understand how to integrate tools into CI, and know when formal proofs are warranted for mission-critical code. Think about a contract you care about: which of these layers would you apply first, and why?

screens.title: What happens during a professional audit
screens.narratorSegment: A professional smart contract security audit is a structured, multi-step examination designed to surface logic flaws, implementation errors, and economic vulnerabilities that automated testing may miss. Start with a manual code review where experienced auditors read every function and examine interface boundaries and state transitions. This manual pass often reveals subtle logic bugs and misuse of Solidity features. Next, auditors apply static analysis tools to quickly find common issues; tools provide a systematic scan but their output is used as an input to human investigation rather than an authoritative verdict. Dynamic analysis and fuzzing come next, exercising the contract with many inputs to trigger unexpected behaviors and state changes. Specialized auditors also perform economic and game-theory analysis to find incentive problems that could let attackers profit. Finally, auditors produce documentation and a prioritized report with severity ratings and concrete remediation suggestions. Audits matter because they combine human intuition with automated breadth; their limitation is cost and the reality that no audit can guarantee zero bugs. When preparing for an audit, provide clear specs, tests, and example scenarios so auditors can focus on the most critical properties. What property do you want audited first for your project?

keyIdea.text: Manual review, static analysis, dynamic testing, economic analysis, and a detailed report together form a comprehensive audit.

content.html:
Core Concept
What happens during a professional audit
A structured sequence of review steps that together offer comprehensive coverage.
Audit Steps
  1. Manual Code Review: Line-by-line inspection to find logic and Solidity-specific pitfalls.
  2. Static Analysis: Automated scans to surface common patterns and candidate vulnerabilities.
  3. Dynamic Analysis / Fuzzing: Stress inputs and explore state to reveal edge cases.
  4. Economic/Game Theory Review: Analyze incentives and attack profitability.
  5. Documentation & Reporting: Prioritized findings and remediation suggestions.
Key Takeaway

An audit combines automated breadth with human insight; prepare clear specs and tests so auditors can focus on your critical properties.

Example: Audit checklist
A sample audit will flag visibility issues, reentrancy points, outdated compiler versions, and economic edge cases, then rank them by severity.
Common-mistake
Assuming an audit is a one-time guarantee. Audits help but do not eliminate risk; plan follow-ups after major changes.
Pro tip
Provide example transactions and a short threat model to help auditors target tests and economic analysis.

screens.title: Static analysis and Slither
screens.narratorSegment: Static analysis examines source code without executing it to find patterns that often indicate vulnerabilities. For Solidity, Slither is a widely used static analysis framework that scans contracts for reentrancy points, missing visibility specifiers, integer issues, and many code smells. Using Slither is straightforward: install via pip and run it against a contract file to get a categorized report. The practical power of Slither is speed and automation — it can scan large codebases quickly and be placed in continuous integration so developers get feedback on every change. But static analysis has limits: it can produce false positives that require human validation, and false negatives where complex business logic or inter-contract behaviors are missed. That is why its output should be read as guidance, not a final verdict. A concrete example is a function flagged for potential reentrancy; Slither will point to patterns like external calls before state updates, but a careful reviewer must confirm whether the calling flow actually exposes a vulnerable path. A common misconception is to believe that a clean static scan means a contract is secure; in practice, combine Slither with testing, fuzzing, and audits to cover different classes of risks. How will you triage a Slither warning in your next review?

content.html:
Static Analysis
Static analysis and Slither
Automated scanning that helps you catch common pitfalls early in development.
Install and run
pip install slither-analyzer
slither path/to/MyContract.sol
Slither outputs categorized findings. Use those categories to prioritize fixes and avoid blocking on low-confidence warnings.
Inspect & triage
  • Validate high-severity warnings first, especially reentrancy and incorrect access control.
  • Mark false positives and document why they are safe for future reviewers.
  • Integrate Slither into CI to catch regressions early.
Common-mistake
Treating a clean Slither report as a guarantee. Always layer with tests, fuzzing, and expert review.

screens.title: Formal verification fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: Formal verification raises the assurance bar by replacing empirical testing with mathematical proof. At its core are three concepts: specification, properties (invariants), and proof. A specification is a precise statement of intended behavior written without ambiguity, often in a formal logic. Properties are conditions that must always hold: for example, that total supply never exceeds a limit, or that only the owner can pause the contract. A proof is a mathematical demonstration that the contract’s code satisfies the specification for all possible inputs and execution paths. Tools such as Certora Prover, K-framework, or general-purpose verifiers like Dafny are used to express properties and attempt proofs. Formal verification can find subtle bugs that neither tests nor audits find, but it is costly and requires expertise: you must formalize the right properties. A common pitfall is proving the wrong property; a correct proof of an incomplete specification leaves gaps. Use formal verification selectively: apply it to protocol core logic or high-value modules where the investment yields meaningful risk reduction. If you were to specify one invariant for your main contract, what would it be and why?

keyIdea.title: Formal proof trade-off
keyIdea.text: Formal verification can prove the absence of specified bugs but requires precise specifications and specialist effort; it is best for core, high-value components.

content.html:
Formal Verification
Formal verification fundamentals
Why mathematical proofs matter for mission-critical logic.
Key terms
  • Specification: Precise description of intended behavior in formal terms.
  • Properties/Invariants: Conditions that must always hold during execution.
  • Proof: Formal demonstration that code satisfies the specification.
Why it matters

Proofs remove ambiguity about behavior across all inputs, which is essential for protocol cores and high-value contracts.

Limits & practice
Formal verification only covers the properties you specify. Missing a critical invariant means the proof won’t catch that risk. Expect high cost and specialized skills.
Concrete example
You might prove that a token's transfer function never changes total supply. That proof does not guarantee that an admin function elsewhere doesn't introduce an unintended mint unless you include that in the specification.

screens.title: Fuzzing and dynamic analysis
screens.narratorSegment: Fuzzing and other dynamic analysis techniques generate diverse and often unexpected inputs to explore program behavior and uncover edge cases that static analysis or tests might miss. In the smart contract context, fuzzers like Echidna or Foundry’s fuzzer will repeatedly call functions with randomized inputs, aiming to violate specified invariants or crash code paths. The value of fuzzing is in exercising state combinations and sequences that a developer might not anticipate. Use fuzzing to complement static checks: static analysis points to suspicious spots while fuzzers try to trigger them in practice. A concrete example is a transfer function that looks correct in tests but when combined with a specific sequence of approvals and callbacks leads to an invariant violation; fuzzing may find that sequence. Common misconceptions include over-trusting fuzzing to find all cases, or expecting it to replace human reasoning — it is an exploration tool that needs targeted properties and time budgets. In practice, add fuzzers to CI or scheduled runs, and combine them with assertions that encode desired invariants. As you tune a fuzzer, ask: which invariants do I want to preserve and how will I detect violations automatically?

content.html:
Process Flow
Fuzzing and dynamic analysis
Automated exploration of inputs and state transitions to find real-world edge cases.
How fuzzing works
  1. Define properties or invariants to check automatically during runs.
  2. Generate and mutate inputs, call contract methods in many sequences.
  3. Record any run that violates an invariant for developer inspection.
Practical notes
Run fuzzers regularly and supply clear invariants. Tune time budgets and seed cases to improve coverage.
Example
A fuzzer finds a sequence of calls that breaks a balance invariant by exercising interleaved deposits and withdrawals combined with an approval flow.

content.html:
Hands-on
Analyze SimpleWallet with Slither
Run the analyzer and learn to interpret findings before fixing code.
Vulnerable SimpleWallet.sol
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract SimpleWallet {
    address public owner;
    mapping(address => uint256) public balances;

    constructor() payable {
        owner = msg.sender;
        balances[msg.sender] = msg.value;
    }

    function deposit() public payable {
        balances[msg.sender] += msg.value;
    }

    // VULNERABLE: Missing access control, anyone can withdraw
    function withdrawAllFunds(address payable _to) public {
        uint256 amount = balances[owner]; // Should be msg.sender, but even then, this is problematic
        require(amount > 0, "No funds to withdraw");
        balances[owner] = 0;
        _to.transfer(amount);
    }

    // VULNERABLE: Reentrancy potential if owner is a malicious contract
    function withdrawMyFunds(uint256 _amount) public {
        require(balances[msg.sender] >= _amount, "Insufficient balance");

        // External call before state update
        (bool success, ) = msg.sender.call{value: _amount}("");
        require(success, "Withdrawal failed");

        balances[msg.sender] -= _amount;
    }

    function getContractBalance() public view returns (uint256) {
        return address(this).balance;
    }
}
Run Slither
pip install slither-analyzer
slither contracts/SimpleWallet.sol
Interpreting results
  • Look for missing access control warnings and reentrancy patterns flagged by Slither.
  • Confirm whether a warning is exploitable given your contract's flows and state assumptions.
Check your understanding
Which Slither finding would you fix first: the missing access control, or the external call before state update? Why?

screens.title: Fixing the wallet: Secure patterns applied
screens.narratorSegment: In this step we apply two concrete secure patterns to the vulnerable wallet. First, fix withdrawAllFunds so only the owner can trigger it and so it withdraws the correct user's balance. That means checking the caller and using the intended account field when reading and zeroing balances. Second, fix withdrawMyFunds using the checks-effects-interactions pattern: validate the caller's balance, update state to deduct the amount, then perform the external transfer. This reorders operations so state changes happen before external calls, preventing reentrancy exploitation of the pre-update balance. After implementing these changes, save the file as SecureWallet. sol and re-run Slither to confirm that the previous warnings are resolved. While Slither may still show low-confidence notes, the two critical warnings — missing access control and external call before state update — should no longer appear. A common misconception is that simply switching to transfer eliminates all reentrancy risk; transfer imposes gas limits but patterns that update state before external calls are the true fix. Once you finish, reflect on how these patterns change the call graph and why they make reentrancy much harder.

content.html:
Hands-on
Fixing the wallet: Secure patterns applied
Implement access control and checks-effects-interactions to remove vulnerabilities.
SecureWallet.sol (excerpt)
// Key fixes: enforce owner checks and apply checks-effects-interactions

function withdrawAllFunds(address payable _to) public {
    require(msg.sender == owner, "Only owner");
    uint256 amount = balances[owner];
    require(amount > 0, "No funds to withdraw");
    balances[owner] = 0;
    (bool success, ) = _to.call{value: amount}("");
    require(success, "Withdrawal failed");
}

function withdrawMyFunds(uint256 _amount) public {
    require(balances[msg.sender] >= _amount, "Insufficient balance");

    // Effects: update state before interaction
    balances[msg.sender] -= _amount;

    // Interaction: external call after state change
    (bool success, ) = msg.sender.call{value: _amount}("");
    require(success, "Withdrawal failed");
}
Run Slither again
slither contracts/SecureWallet.sol
If the fixes are correct, Slither should no longer flag the missing access control and the specific reentrancy pattern. Document remaining low-confidence warnings and why they are safe or prepare follow-up changes.
Key Takeaway
Apply checks-effects-interactions and explicit access checks; verify with static tools, but keep human review for logic and incentives.

screens.title: Tools and their roles
screens.narratorSegment: Different security techniques serve different needs; choosing the right combination is a risk-based decision. Static analysis like Slither is fast and automated, ideal for early feedback on common mistakes and for CI. Fuzzing and dynamic analysis explore runtime behavior and find stateful edge cases that static tools may miss. Professional audits add human expertise and economic reasoning, useful before major deployments or for complex protocols. Formal verification offers the strongest guarantee for the properties you specify, but it is expensive and specialized. Use cases: for a simple NFT contract, thorough testing, Slither, and a modest bug bounty may be sufficient. For a core lending protocol handling large pools, perform audits and consider formal verification on core accounting invariants. A common error is selecting tools in isolation: do not assume passing one layer means others are unnecessary. A layered pipeline gives better coverage: automated scans on every commit, fuzzing day/night runs, scheduled audits prior to mainnet, and targeted formal proofs for protocol cores. screens.title: Limits and common mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the limits of each approach prevents misplaced confidence. Static analysis is fast but can miss logic tied to business rules or contract interactions; it also produces false positives that waste time if not triaged. Audits add human insight and economic reasoning, but they cost money and still may miss novel attack patterns or future protocol changes. Fuzzers explore runtime behavior but depend on the properties you check and the time budget you give them. Formal verification delivers strong guarantees only for the properties you specify; it cannot protect against requirements that were never formalized. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we’ll explore the advanced layers of smart contract assurance that go beyond normal unit testing. You already know how to write tests, but tests only show the presence of a bug under specific inputs. Here we will study professional audits, automated static analysis with tools like Slither, dynamic tools such as fuzzers, and the highest-assurance approach: formal verification. You will learn what each technique promises, where it fits in the development lifecycle, and the trade-offs — cost, time, required expertise, and types of bugs each method is best at finding. We’ll also follow a small hands-on workflow: run Slither on a deliberately vulnerable wallet contract, interpret the findings, apply fixes using secure patterns, and re-run tools to confirm remediation. By the end of this chapter you’ll be able to choose which measures are appropriate for different risk levels, understand how to integrate tools into CI, and know when formal proofs are warranted for mission-critical code. Think about a contract you care about: which of these layers would you apply first, and why?

This chapter equips you with practical judgment and concrete skills for securing Solidity contracts beyond unit tests. First, you will learn the role and value of professional security audits: how expert reviewers combine manual inspection, economic analysis, and tooling to find subtle logic and incentive flaws. Second, you will identify and use static analysis tools like Slither, understanding how automated scans complement human review and how to interpret tool output including false positives. Third, you will grasp the core ideas of formal verification: writing precise specifications and proving properties so critical behaviors hold on every execution path. Finally, you will explore the limitations of auditing and automation, and learn how to integrate these tools into a development workflow for continuous security assurance. Each objective ties to a practical activity in this chapter: running Slither on a vulnerable wallet, applying secure fixes, and reflecting on when audits or formal proofs are necessary. By the end you’ll be able to choose appropriate measures for different risk profiles and explain their unique contributions to security.

Beyond concepts, this chapter pushes you to adopt concrete habits. You will learn to run Slither locally and in CI, to read and triage static analysis findings, and to prioritize fixes. You will practice secure coding patterns such as checks-effects-interactions to avoid reentrancy, and you will learn how fuzzing fills gaps left by static scanning. You will also learn when to call for professional audits and how audits complement automated tools by evaluating game-theoretic risks and unusual attack vectors. Finally, you will explore how to operate continuous security: run static analysis on every commit, fuzz regularly, and run follow-up audits after significant changes. These practices turn security from a checklist into a living process. As you work through the hands-on activity in this chapter, aim to form a short, repeatable pipeline you can apply to your projects: automated scans, tests, fuzzing, and scheduled reviews or bounties.

A professional smart contract security audit is a structured, multi-step examination designed to surface logic flaws, implementation errors, and economic vulnerabilities that automated testing may miss. Start with a manual code review where experienced auditors read every function and examine interface boundaries and state transitions. This manual pass often reveals subtle logic bugs and misuse of Solidity features. Next, auditors apply static analysis tools to quickly find common issues; tools provide a systematic scan but their output is used as an input to human investigation rather than an authoritative verdict. Dynamic analysis and fuzzing come next, exercising the contract with many inputs to trigger unexpected behaviors and state changes. Specialized auditors also perform economic and game-theory analysis to find incentive problems that could let attackers profit. Finally, auditors produce documentation and a prioritized report with severity ratings and concrete remediation suggestions. Audits matter because they combine human intuition with automated breadth; their limitation is cost and the reality that no audit can guarantee zero bugs. When preparing for an audit, provide clear specs, tests, and example scenarios so auditors can focus on the most critical properties. What property do you want audited first for your project?

Static analysis examines source code without executing it to find patterns that often indicate vulnerabilities. For Solidity, Slither is a widely used static analysis framework that scans contracts for reentrancy points, missing visibility specifiers, integer issues, and many code smells. Using Slither is straightforward: install via pip and run it against a contract file to get a categorized report. The practical power of Slither is speed and automation — it can scan large codebases quickly and be placed in continuous integration so developers get feedback on every change. But static analysis has limits: it can produce false positives that require human validation, and false negatives where complex business logic or inter-contract behaviors are missed. That is why its output should be read as guidance, not a final verdict. A concrete example is a function flagged for potential reentrancy; Slither will point to patterns like external calls before state updates, but a careful reviewer must confirm whether the calling flow actually exposes a vulnerable path. A common misconception is to believe that a clean static scan means a contract is secure; in practice, combine Slither with testing, fuzzing, and audits to cover different classes of risks. How will you triage a Slither warning in your next review?

Formal verification raises the assurance bar by replacing empirical testing with mathematical proof. At its core are three concepts: specification, properties (invariants), and proof. A specification is a precise statement of intended behavior written without ambiguity, often in a formal logic. Properties are conditions that must always hold: for example, that total supply never exceeds a limit, or that only the owner can pause the contract. A proof is a mathematical demonstration that the contract’s code satisfies the specification for all possible inputs and execution paths. Tools such as Certora Prover, K-framework, or general-purpose verifiers like Dafny are used to express properties and attempt proofs. Formal verification can find subtle bugs that neither tests nor audits find, but it is costly and requires expertise: you must formalize the right properties. A common pitfall is proving the wrong property; a correct proof of an incomplete specification leaves gaps. Use formal verification selectively: apply it to protocol core logic or high-value modules where the investment yields meaningful risk reduction. If you were to specify one invariant for your main contract, what would it be and why?

Fuzzing and other dynamic analysis techniques generate diverse and often unexpected inputs to explore program behavior and uncover edge cases that static analysis or tests might miss. In the smart contract context, fuzzers like Echidna or Foundry’s fuzzer will repeatedly call functions with randomized inputs, aiming to violate specified invariants or crash code paths. The value of fuzzing is in exercising state combinations and sequences that a developer might not anticipate. Use fuzzing to complement static checks: static analysis points to suspicious spots while fuzzers try to trigger them in practice. A concrete example is a transfer function that looks correct in tests but when combined with a specific sequence of approvals and callbacks leads to an invariant violation; fuzzing may find that sequence. Common misconceptions include over-trusting fuzzing to find all cases, or expecting it to replace human reasoning — it is an exploration tool that needs targeted properties and time budgets. In practice, add fuzzers to CI or scheduled runs, and combine them with assertions that encode desired invariants. As you tune a fuzzer, ask: which invariants do I want to preserve and how will I detect violations automatically?

We're going to walk through a practical example: a vulnerable SimpleWallet contract that intentionally contains two problems — a withdrawal function lacking proper access control and another function with a reentrancy risk. First, save the provided contract in your Hardhat contracts directory. Install Slither via pip if you haven't, and run Slither pointing to the contract file. Slither will list findings grouped by category; key warnings to watch for include missing access control on critical functions and patterns where external calls happen before state updates. When you see a warning, read the code snippet Slither references and ask whether the call path actually allows an attacker to change state unexpectedly. A common mistake is to ignore warnings because they seem noisy; instead, triage them: confirm high-severity issues immediately and document false positives. This hands-on run teaches interpretation more than the command itself. The concrete exercise prepares you to make precise fixes that we’ll apply in the next screen and then re-run Slither to confirm remediation.
